Repository: re-cinq/HALEngine
Ticket: #94 Run onError and afterSession when beforeSession throws

You are editing files in a git repository. Your job is to define DONE for
the ticket below as executable acceptance tests that FAIL right now, so
that "these are green" and "this ticket is finished" mean the same thing.

The ticket's branch is checked out with write access at /var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/07ecb52f78e0/workspace/target.
Run every command from inside it (`cd /var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/07ecb52f78e0/workspace/target` first). The ticket
is at `/var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/07ecb52f78e0/workspace/ticket.md`: read it before anything else. Pass `repo` (the
owner/name your task names above) on every `lore_*` call: the gateway has
no checkout to detect it from.

You write tests. You write no production code at all.

START by reading the spec this ticket belongs to, if it names one. A
spec's UN-LINKED testable statements — the ones carrying no
`([validated by ...])` parenthetical — are your work list: one acceptance
test each. A ticket with no spec is defined by its own text instead.

THE CONTRACT, NON-NEGOTIABLE:
- Write the smallest set of acceptance tests such that all of them passing
  means the ticket is done and nothing more is owed. Prefer one; three is
  a lot; more than five means the ticket needs splitting, not testing.
- Put them in a NEW test file of their own, beside the code, never
  appended to an existing test file. Its name MUST end in
  `.acceptance.test.<ext>` — `repo-settings.acceptance.test.ts`,
  `Plan.acceptance.test.tsx` — so a reader and the tooling can tell an
  acceptance test from a round's own at a glance. Later rounds write their own tests and run
  only those; the pod's Bash hook refuses the files listed under "Done
  when these pass" by name, so an acceptance test sharing a file with
  theirs would lock them out of their own test.
- RUN them — those, and nothing else. Not the repository's full suite,
  not lint, not the typechecker, not the formatter.
  CI is the judge of this branch and runs all of it on every push.
  Name the test files you run: the pod's Bash hook refuses a bare
  `npm test` or a `vitest run` with no path.
  Every acceptance test must fail, and fail for the RIGHT reason — the
  behaviour is absent, not the import path typo'd or a fixture missing.
- Quote the actual failure output in your final message. A test you did
  not run is not a red bar, it is a guess — unless this pod cannot run
  it at all, below.
- Do not weaken, skip or `.todo` a test to make the suite tidy. Red is the
  deliverable.

WHEN THIS POD CANNOT RUN THE TESTS. The pod carries Node and a few tools,
not every language's toolchain. If the command that runs your tests is
missing here — `java`, `mvn`, `gradle`, `go`, `cargo` or `dotnet` is not
found, or a wrapper such as `./mvnw` reports no `JAVA_HOME` — do not look
for it and do not install it: no `sudo`, no `apt`, no `find /`, no
download. The pull request's CI runs these tests on every push and proves
the red bar instead. Write the tests as the contract says, read each one
against the ticket's claim in place of running it, then commit and push.
In `.lore/dod.md`, right under the strategy, write that the red bar is
CI's to show and name the CI job that runs the tests. In your final
message, quote the command CI runs where the failure output would be.

WHAT AN ACCEPTANCE TEST IS. It observes behaviour through the code's
real entry point — a function called, a component rendered, a binary
run. A test whose assertion subject is the repository's own source text
(readFileSync of a src/ or test file, a regex over another test, counting
occurrences of a literal across files) is NOT an acceptance test and you
must not write one; it pins prose, not behaviour, and it outlives the
ticket as noise. The honest moves instead:
- "This prose drifts from a value" — make the prose compute the value
  (interpolate the count into the title, derive the label from the
  fixture). Drift becomes impossible; no guard file exists.
- "This duplication must not come back" — the diff removing it and the
  existing tests staying green are the proof; a scan test is not.
- If the only red bar you can build is a test about source text, the
  ticket owes no new test at all — that is what `mechanical` is for.

SCOPE FIDELITY, EQUALLY NON-NEGOTIABLE. The ticket below carries the
issue's title AND body — the reported problem is in there, not in your
reading of it:
- Open `.lore/dod.md` by QUOTING the ticket's central claim, verbatim.
  The claim is what the reporter says is wrong, in their words.
- Every acceptance test must fail BECAUSE of that claim. Run each red
  test and read its failure output against the quote: failing for a
  reason the ticket never states means you have redefined the ticket,
  and a merged PR built on it closes the report without fixing it.
  That is `changes_requested`, not a DoD.
- A neighbouring problem you notice on the way is a finding for your
  final message, never a substitute subject for the tests.
- A bulk mechanical fix across hundreds of sites is "really several
  tickets": park it via the `changes_requested` line below rather than
  shrinking it into the slice you can express.

TRIAGE — pick exactly one strategy and say which:
- `direct` — a seam already exists. The acceptance test can call the real
  entry point today and fail on behaviour. Use this whenever it is honest.
- `parallel-change` — no seam, but the change has a boundary. Build the
  replacement BESIDE the existing code: point the acceptance tests at the
  NEW module, leave the old code untouched and running while the new one
  is red, and switch callers over only once it is green. The FIRST test
  must go through the real caller path into the new module, even if that
  module handles one case and throws on the rest — a replacement that is
  not wired up drifts from the thing it replaces.
- `characterize` — no seam and the change is diffuse. Do NOT write the
  ticket's acceptance tests yet. First pin the CURRENT behaviour with
  characterization tests that pass NOW, commit that green bar, and write
  the ticket's acceptance tests against it. A refactor without a green bar
  underneath it is not a refactor. The `legacy-characterize` skill is the
  contract for this.
- `mechanical` — the ticket is a small, fully-specified edit that owes no
  new permanent test: a wrong label or count in prose, a doc correction,
  a dedup whose behaviour EXISTING tests already pin. The DoD is the edit
  itself plus those named existing tests staying green — name them under
  Acceptance tests, RUN them, and quote that they PASS today. Write no
  new test; the diff and the green bar are the proof, and the review
  judges the edit. Do not stretch this onto a ticket that changes
  behaviour: if no existing test pins what the edit touches, the ticket
  is not mechanical.

Record the triage in `.lore/dod.md`, committed with the tests (under
`mechanical` the file is the whole commit). Write it for the next pod,
which has your branch and none of your reasoning — and for the human who
opens the branch to see where the ticket stands. Use EXACTLY this shape.
It is markdown and it is read rendered: the blank lines are what keep the
claim, the strategy and the tests from collapsing into one paragraph, and
the checkboxes are what make a round's progress legible at a glance.
No emoji, no decoration; the structure is what makes it readable.
  # Definition of Done

  > <the ticket's central claim, quoted verbatim>

  **Strategy: `direct`** — <one or two sentences: what seam exists or does
  not. One of direct | parallel-change | characterize | mechanical.>

  ## Done when these pass

  - [ ] **<test name>** — <the behaviour it pins; under `mechanical`, the
    EXISTING tests that must stay green>
    `path/to/test.ts`

  ## Facets

  - [ ] <the red-green-refactor steps you expect, smallest first; under
    `mechanical`, the exact edits owed. One line each. A round ticks the
    box it closed rather than rewriting the list.>

  ## Out of scope

  - <what this ticket does NOT cover>

TRACEABILITY:
- Each test validates a statement in a spec or ADR. Add the inline
  parenthetical on that statement in the repository's established form —
  `Statement. ([validated by name](path/to/test.ts#L42))`. Inserting a
  test shifts every #Lnn link below it: when the repository has
  `scripts/spec-links/reanchor.mjs`, run
  `node scripts/spec-links/reanchor.mjs` from the repository root after
  the formatter — it moves each link to its test's current line, by test
  title, and prints the links it could not map, which you fix by hand.
  Without it, re-verify every existing #Lnn link on the statements you
  touch yourself.
- Stamp the test's spec anchor (the "specs/<path>#<ordinal>" it
  validates) so the repo's tests.list surfaces it as the descriptor's
  `spec` field and the VALIDATED_BY link is established automatically —
  see `.lore/test-commands.yml` for how this repo exposes descriptors.

RULES:
- Use your Read tool to read files before editing. Read the existing tests
  first — mirror their framework, directory, file suffix and naming.
- No mocks, no stubs. Exercise real values. A behaviour that seems to need
  a double is telling you where the seam is missing; say so in
  `.lore/dod.md` and pick `parallel-change` or `characterize` accordingly.
- Write no production code. Not a stub, not a signature, not a TODO.
- Do not edit `| Status |` on any spec. Nothing is implemented yet.

DELIVERY, NON-NEGOTIABLE — the next step runs in a DIFFERENT container:
- Before you commit, run the repository's FORMATTER over the files you
  changed (`npx prettier --write <files>`, `gofmt -w <files>`, whichever
  this repo uses) and nothing else from CI's checklist. Do NOT run the
  linter in this pod: CI runs it on every push, and here it does not
  fit — in this repository a two-file `eslint` peaks near 800 MB against
  a 1Gi pod, and runs 112256d9 and 62c1ca5e were OOM-killed on exactly
  that. A lint finding comes back as a red build naming the file and
  line, which the next round fixes with an editor.
- Do NOT typecheck here either. A green test is not a compiled build —
  vitest transpiles each file without checking types — but CI's build
  step is what proves it, and in this repository `tsc --noEmit` on
  `libs/shared` peaks near 950 MB against the 1Gi pod: run 2a291314's
  dod pod was OOM-killed on it. A type error comes back as a red build
  whose failed step and log tail name the file and line; the next
  round fixes it there. Read your imports and signatures twice instead.
- NEVER run a workspace build in this pod (`npm run build`, `tsc -b`, a
  `tsc` without `--noEmit`): tests resolve every workspace package from
  SOURCE, so nothing needs building for a test to see your change, and
  the build is the 950 MB step that OOM-killed run abac6ee9 while it
  rebuilt libs/shared for a test that never needed it.
- When the work is done, `git -C /var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/07ecb52f78e0/workspace/target add` what you changed and commit it with a
  short, factual message. Then `git -C /var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/07ecb52f78e0/workspace/target push origin HEAD`. The clone carries
  its own credentials, so a plain push authenticates; you need no token
  and must never look for one.
- Then bring the branch up to date with its base — `git fetch origin main`
  and merge `origin/main` in — and push again if that produced anything.
  A branch that cannot merge cleanly gets NO CI AT ALL: GitHub runs no
  workflow on a conflicted pull request, so the ticket parks on a build
  that will never start. Resolve any conflict now, favouring `origin/main`
  for anything this ticket did not write, and never by discarding your own
  work. This is why a nine-day-old branch stalled: 186 commits of drift,
  no checks, and a wait with nothing to wait for.
- Confirm it landed: `git status` must report the branch is not ahead of
  its upstream. An unpushed commit lives only in this container and
  dies with it — do NOT report success for one.
- If you genuinely changed nothing, say why and end your final message
  with the line `LORE_NODE_RESULT: {"outcome":"failed"}` so the line does
  not validate an empty branch — unless the ticket is already resolved,
  which has its own line below.
- Do not open a pull request: you have no `gh` and no GitHub token. Lore
  opens the PR from the branch you push.

THE LAST LINE YOU PRINT decides where this ticket goes. Print exactly one,
on its own line, as the final thing in your message:
- Red acceptance tests are committed and pushed — or, under `mechanical`,
  `.lore/dod.md` naming green existing tests is (state the strategy you
  picked in the extra):
  LORE_NODE_RESULT: {"outcome":"success","extras":{"dod_strategy":"direct"}}
- The ticket cannot be expressed as acceptance tests that fail for ITS
  stated reason — it is ambiguous, it is really several tickets (a bulk
  mechanical fix included), it asks for something unobservable, or every
  honest red test you can write fails for a reason the ticket never
  states. Say precisely what you would need, then:
  LORE_NODE_RESULT: {"outcome":"changes_requested","extras":{"dod_blocked":"<one line: what is missing>"}}
  This parks the ticket for a human. It is the right answer for a bad
  ticket and the wrong answer for a hard one. The dod_blocked line is
  posted verbatim on the issue as the request for a rewrite, so write it
  for the ticket's author: what is missing, not what you tried.
- The ticket's central claim is ALREADY TRUE on the branch's base: the
  behaviour it asks for is present on `origin/main` (a merged sibling
  pull request, a commit naming the issue), so no honest red test
  exists and nothing is owed. Write no tests and commit nothing. Name
  what resolved it — the commit or pull request — then:
  LORE_NODE_RESULT: {"outcome":"changes_requested","extras":{"dod_resolved":"<one line: what already resolved it, naming the commit or PR>"}}
  This CLOSES the ticket and its draft pull request, with your line
  posted as the reason, so write it for whoever reads the issue later.
  A ticket that is partly done is not resolved: that is a DoD for the
  remaining part, not this line.

commit 4c26b5f0852635d8ce5d31ca59af7a7eecc23ea9
Author: vvondruska <2923801+vvondruska@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Wed Oct 7 10:01:43 2026 +0200

    feat(transport): answer a client's conversation list over the socket (#152)
    
    * feat(transport): answer a client's conversation list over the socket
    
    #143 gave the store listFor; nothing reached a client with it, so every
    consumer would have stood up its own authenticated route over data the
    engine already authenticates on the upgrade.
    
    Adds two additive frames - list_conversations and conversation_list -
    behind transport.history, off by default and deliberately not folded into
    transport.resume: rejoining hands a client back a conversation it was in,
    a list tells it what else the user has, and a deployer who agreed to the
    first did not agree to the second. A test pins that resume on with
    history off still refuses.
    
    The frame names no user and has no field for one: the id comes from the
    connection. It is answered off the per-session lock, so a list sent while
    an answer streams arrives before that answer ends.
    
    A frame this server does not serve is answered UNSUPPORTED, new in
    ErrorCodes, and never an empty list - a client cannot tell "no
    conversations" from "the server could not look". A failing store answers
    SERVER_ERROR carrying none of its words, and the log takes the error's
    type rather than its message, as the authenticator path already does,
    because a driver's message can hold a connection string and its password.
    
    Two departures from the issue's plan, both forced by #143's review: the
    frame's `before` carries updatedAt and sessionId rather than a bare
    timestamp, since a cursor on a time alone skips a conversation when two
    share one; and the validator dispatches through a Map rather than a
    switch, so a frame typed `constructor` misses instead of reaching an
    inherited member.
    
    Closes #144
    
    * fix(transport): prove the list is answered off the turn lock
    
    An independent review found the branch's headline concurrency claim
    resting on a vacuous assertion, and five smaller faults.
    
    The ordering test compared indexOf against indexOf, and indexOf is -1
    when the frame never arrives, so -1 < any index passed. It passed with
    history switched off entirely, and would have passed with the list queued
    behind the lock. It now holds the turn open with a deferred release that
    only fires once the list has been answered, and asserts the list arrived
    exactly once, between two of the turn's own deltas. Queueing it behind
    the lock now fails the test, which was checked by doing it.
    
    A list_conversations could also be answered with silence: the handler
    served it only when its deps were present, and createMessageHandler takes
    them optionally. A handler with no store now answers UNSUPPORTED like any
    other server that cannot serve the frame, so the engine has no silent
    frame left. reportInvalid narrows its argument, which removes a guard
    that could never run.
    
    MongoSessionStore now throws the exported StoreCannotList for a
    collection injected without a find, and the transport answers that
    UNSUPPORTED rather than SERVER_ERROR, logging it by name: a permanent
    misconfiguration no longer reads as a transient database failure.
    
    A list is also useless without resume, since ?sessionId= is read only
    under it, so the engine warns at startup for that combination and the
    docs no longer promise a row can be opened without it. The docs now say
    the connection's own conversation is listed like any other, and the
    changelog has one Added section whose listFor entry no longer claims
    nothing serves it.
    
    Refs #144
    
    * test(transport): close the gaps against the issue's criteria
    
    An audit of the branch against #144's acceptance criteria found five
    things asked for and not delivered.
    
    The criteria wanted a fixture pinning that every frame valid before this
    change still compiles. src/types/messagesAdditive.test.ts is it, typed as
    the unions so a required field added to any existing frame fails tsc
    there - confirmed by adding one to EntryDeltaMessage and watching it
    fail. The validator tests asserted only that a bad limit or cursor was
    refused, not that the error names the field, which the criteria asked for
    and the code already does.
    
    "Exactly one conversation_list, and no stream_end" went unasserted,
    because the helper resolved on the first matching frame and counted
    nothing. The answer is now fenced by a ping sent once the list has
    arrived - a ping is answered synchronously and would otherwise overtake a
    list that awaits the store - so the whole frame set is asserted.
    
    The failure log carried the user id but not the session id, which every
    other ws line carries and which is what ties a failure to its connection.
    
    ConversationHistoryOptions now mirrors SessionResumeOptions' retention
    note, pointing at #41: a list reaches as far back as the store keeps
    conversations, and that bound is the consumer's.
    
    Refs #144
    
    * fix(transport): make the list's own tests able to fail
    
    A third review, with no context on the first two, found four things.
    
    The spec said a list arriving mid-turn lands "after one of the turn's
    deltas". Measured, it lands after the turn's user entry and before the
    assistant entry, and the test only asserted a position greater than zero.
    The sentence now says what happens and the test asserts the whole frame
    order, which the deferred release makes deterministic.
    
    The additivity fixture asserted a literal against itself: making
    ConnectedMessage.resumed required left it green, and only tsc went red.
    It now drives the real validator and the real sender, so a frame that
    stops being read or stops going out intact fails it - checked by breaking
    both. It moves to src/transport/ws/, since a test under src/types/ may
    not import the transport layer, and the two spec statements now claim
    what a test run proves rather than what the compiler does.
    
    onTheWire called toISOString on a value the type says is a Date, so a
    store answering the ISO strings the wire shows got an opaque
    SERVER_ERROR, while the cursor beside it deliberately accepts a string
    for the same reason. It maps through `new Date` now. Removing the mapper
    entirely used to leave every test green, because JSON.stringify
    serialises a Date the same way; a store answering an epoch number now
    tells the two apart.
    
    One socket could also turn frames sent in a tick into that many parallel
    store reads: fifty frames, fifty in flight, measured. Reads are
    serialised per socket now - ten frames, ten answers, one query at a time.
    
    Refs #144
    
    * test(transport): cover the path that keeps a socket unwedged
    
    The per-socket read chain swallows a rejection so one failed answer does
    not reject every list queued behind it, and nothing reached that line:
    answerOne catches its own failures, so the only way out is a send that
    throws and a report of it that throws too. A socket failing both now
    proves the next list is still answered, and conversationList.ts is back
    to full coverage.
    
    Refs #144
    
    * docs(transport): stop crediting the dispatch table with an old property
    
    The spec said the validator's Map is why a frame typed `constructor`
    reads as unknown. Checked by restoring the switch it replaced: that
    passes the same test, so the Map fixed nothing there - an object keyed by
    the frame's own type would have been the unsafe shape, and the table is a
    Map for that reason. The sentence says so now.
    
    The protocol spec's failure statement also names the user id as personal
    data, since that log line carries one.
    
    Separately, the log capture stays quiet through teardown instead of
    restoring the noisy default: a socket closing after its own test made
    jest report "Cannot log after tests are done", three times across the run
    and now once, in a suite that installs no capture.
    
    Refs #144
    
    * fix(transport): blame a failed send on the socket, not the store
    
    A send that threw was caught by the same block as the store read, so a
    dead socket was logged and answered as a store failure. Only the read and
    the mapping of what it answered sit in the try now; the send follows it,
    and a throw there is reported as handling the message. The test asserts
    the log line, so putting the send back inside the try fails it.
    
    A client naming ?sessionId= while resume is off also got silence: the id
    is simply not read, so a client that took it from a conversation list
    opens an empty session with nothing said. The engine warns the first time
    that happens, once per engine rather than once per upgrade, since the line
    is a deployment fault and a per-upgrade one could be flooded by anybody.
    
    Telling the client instead was considered and rejected: a `connected`
    frame with resume off is byte-for-byte what it was before resume existed,
    which the resume spec states and a test pins, and this is not worth
    breaking that for.
    
    Refs #144
    
    * refactor(transport): share one page bound instead of two that agree
    
    A fourth review, context-free like the others, found five minor things.
    
    The validator kept its own MAX_PAGE of 200 beside the store's MAX_LIMIT of
    200, with a code comment and a spec sentence both asserting they agree and
    nothing holding them to it: raising one left the other refusing 201 and
    verify green. The store's constant is exported and the validator imports
    it, so there is one bound and nothing to drift.
    
    The transport rebuilds each row from four fields, which is what stops a
    custom listFor answering whole sessions from putting entries, credentials
    or another user's id on the wire. Nothing tested it, under a feature whose
    spec leans on that strip for its GDPR paragraph. A store answering a whole
    session now proves the wire carries four keys and none of its secrets.
    
    The ignored-session-id warning fires whether or not history is on, so an
    existing install with resume off and clients that append an id sees a new
    warn line: that is consumer-observable and now has a CHANGELOG entry, and
    the docs explain it under Session Resume where ?sessionId= is documented
    rather than only under Conversation List.
    
    Also: the README's transport block lists `history` beside `resume`, the
    once-per-engine suppression is pinned as per-engine rather than
    per-process, and storeOfThree drops a cast that would have broken silently
    if the store's create became async.
    
    Refs #144

parameters.content:
# Definition of Done

> `beforeSession` is awaited before the `try` block opens, so a throw from it escapes before the `catch` and `finally` exist. Neither `onError` nor `afterSession` runs.

**Strategy: `direct`** — `createChatOrchestrator` accepts `OrchestratorHooks` directly and `processMessage` drives the real turn lifecycle, so the acceptance test calls `processMessage` with a throwing `beforeSession` hook and fails on the absent `onError` and `afterSession` invocations today.

## Done when these pass

- [ ] **runs onError and afterSession and rethrows when beforeSession throws** — When `beforeSession` throws an `Error`, `onError` is called with `(session, error)`, `afterSession` is called with `(session)` after `onError`, neither `beforeUserInput` nor the provider runs, and `processMessage` still rejects with the thrown error.
  `src/orchestration/beforeSessionThrow.acceptance.test.ts`

## Facets

- [ ] Move `if (hooks?.beforeSession) await hooks.beforeSession(session);` inside the `try` block in `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` so a throw reaches `catch` (`onError`) and `finally` (`afterSession`).
- [ ] Add a `CHANGELOG.md` entry under `## [Unreleased]` describing the behaviour change for existing consumers whose `afterSession` and `onError` hooks now run when `beforeSession` throws.

## Out of scope

- The `instanceof Error` gate on `onError` when a non-`Error` value is thrown.
- Summing token usage across tool rounds in `afterModelResponse` (HALEngine#93).
